lessons.unit: 9A: Genetics and evolution
lessons.title: Variation: continuous and discontinuous
lessons.bigQuestion: Why is no one in the world exactly like you?
objectives: Describe variation within and between species
Distinguish continuous and discontinuous variation
Choose suitable graphs for each type
successCriteria: Give examples of variation within a species
Classify features as continuous or discontinuous
Draw a histogram or bar chart and explain the choice
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: histograms and bar charts; Islamic Studies: diversity of creation (Surah Ar-Rum 30:22)
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: diversity of human tongues and colours as a sign (Ar-Rum 30:22); social: respecting difference

keywords.def: differences between living things
organisms that can breed to produce fertile offspring
can take any value in a range, e.g. height
falls into distinct groups, e.g. blood group

starter: Bismillah. Name a feature you share with a family member
Draw a quick bar chart axis

teach.heading: Within and between species
bullets: Between: a cat and a dog
teach.note: Answer the big question partly. Identical twins share genes but still differ through environment.

teach.heading: Two types of variation
teach.note: Classify features as a class: height, eye colour, mass, blood group, tongue rolling, hand span.

model.problem: Class hand spans (cm): 16–17: 3; 17–18: 7; 18–19: 9; 19–20: 5; 20–21: 1. Which graph and why?
steps: Hand span is measured: continuous
Use a histogram with touching bars
Shape: most in the middle, fewer at the extremes

teach.heading: Eye colour is tricky
teach.note: Shows that real data can be messy.

misconception.wrong: Height is discontinuous because we round it
misconception.right: Height can take any value; rounding doesn't change its type

check.q: Which is discontinuous variation?
check.why: Blood group is A, B, AB or O: distinct groups. The others are measured on a continuous scale.

practice: Classify: shoe size, skin colour, blood group, arm length
Which graph for blood group data?
Give one example of variation between species
independent: Core: Draw a bar chart of blood groups in a sample: O 22, A 20, B 6, AB 2
Extend: Draw a histogram of a class's heights from given data and describe its shape
Stretch: Explain why shoe size data looks discontinuous even though foot length is continuous.
exit: Is hand span continuous or discontinuous?
lessons.homework: Measure the hand spans of five family members and record whether each has attached or free earlobes. Identify the type of each.
lessons.send: Support: sorting cards. Stretch: normal distribution.

lessons.unit: 9A: Genetics and evolution
lessons.title: Inherited and environmental variation
lessons.bigQuestion: Is your accent in your genes?
objectives: Distinguish inherited and environmental variation
Explain features caused by both
Use twin studies as evidence
successCriteria: Classify features as inherited, environmental or both
Explain how environment can change inherited features
Use identical twin data to draw conclusions
lessons.crossCurricular: PE: training and fitness; English: accents and dialects
lessons.smsc: Moral: we are responsible for what we can change (effort, character)

keywords.def: caused by genes passed from parents
caused by surroundings and lifestyle
twins from one fertilised egg with the same genes
a feature of an organism

starter: What is a gene (your best guess)?

teach.heading: Three categories
bullets: Inherited: blood group, natural eye colour
teach.note: Answer the big question: accent is environmental (learned).

teach.heading: Twin studies
bullets: Twins raised apart are especially useful

model.problem: Identical twins raised apart differ in mass by 6 kg; in height by 1 cm. What does this suggest?
steps: Same genes, so differences come from environment
Mass differs a lot: strongly affected by diet and exercise
Height differs little: mostly controlled by genes
model.answer: Height is mainly genetic; mass is strongly environmental

teach.heading: Plants too
bullets: Same seeds, different light → different heights
Hydrangea flower colour changes with soil pH
teach.note: Good examples of environmental effects on inherited potential.

misconception.right: Genes set a range; diet and health affect where you end up

check.q: Which feature is purely environmental?
check.why: Language is learned. Hair colour and blood group are inherited; height is both.

practice: Classify: tattoo, eye colour, mass, dimples
Why are identical twins useful to scientists?
Give one feature affected by both
independent: Core: Sort twelve features into inherited, environmental and both, with reasons
Extend: Plan an experiment with cuttings of one plant to show environmental variation
Stretch: Evaluate twin studies: what can they tell us, and what are their limitations?
exit: Why do identical twins have the same genes?
Is mass inherited, environmental or both?
lessons.homework: Interview a family member: list three features they inherited and three that came from their environment or choices.
lessons.send: Support: sorting grid. Stretch: epigenetics preview.

lessons.unit: 9A: Genetics and evolution
lessons.title: Chromosomes, genes and inheritance
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do children look a bit like each parent but not exactly like either?
objectives: Describe the relationship between DNA, genes and chromosomes
Explain how genetic material is passed on in fertilisation
Explain why siblings differ
successCriteria: Put nucleus, chromosome, gene and DNA in order of size
Explain why gametes have half the chromosomes
Explain variation between siblings using fertilisation
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: probability; RE/Islamic Studies: lineage (nasab) and its importance
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the creation of each person in the womb (Surah Al-Mu'minun 23:12–14)

keywords.def: a long strand of DNA in the nucleus
a section of DNA that codes for a characteristic
a sex cell: sperm or egg
fusion of a sperm and egg nucleus

starter: Where is genetic material found in a cell?

teach.heading: From nucleus to gene
teach.note: Use the library analogy: nucleus = library, chromosomes = books, genes = recipes, DNA = the letters.

model.problem: Explain why a child is not identical to either parent
steps: Each gamete has half the chromosomes
Each gamete gets a random mix of the parent's chromosomes
Fertilisation joins two random gametes
So the child has a new combination of genes
model.answer: A unique mix of genes from both parents

teach.heading: Brothers and sisters differ
bullets: Each sperm and egg has a different mix
teach.note: Except identical twins (one fertilised egg splits).

misconception.right: Gametes have 23 so that fertilisation restores 46

check.q: How many chromosomes are in a human egg cell?
check.why: Gametes carry one of each pair: 23. Body cells carry 46.

practice: Order by size: gene, nucleus, chromosome
How many chromosomes in a human skin cell?
What happens at fertilisation?
independent: Core: Draw and label a diagram from cell to gene
Extend: Dogs have 78 chromosomes in body cells. How many in a dog sperm? Explain
Stretch: Explain why identical twins have the same genes but non-identical twins do not.
lessons.homework: Make a model of a chromosome showing genes as coloured sections, with a label key.
lessons.send: Support: library analogy card. Stretch: sex chromosomes XX/XY.

lessons.unit: 9A: Genetics and evolution
lessons.title: DNA: structure and discovery
lessons.bigQuestion: Who really discovered the structure of DNA?
objectives: Describe the structure of DNA
Describe the work of Franklin, Wilkins, Watson and Crick
Explain how scientific ideas develop through collaboration and evidence
successCriteria: Describe DNA as a double helix with bases
Explain each scientist's contribution
Evaluate whether credit was shared fairly
lessons.crossCurricular: History: science in the 1950s; English: discussing fairness and ethics
lessons.smsc: Moral: fairness and honesty in giving credit (avoiding injustice, zulm)

keywords.def: deoxyribonucleic acid: the molecule that carries genetic code
the twisted-ladder shape of DNA
a chemical 'letter' of DNA: A, T, C or G
using X-rays to find the shape of molecules

teach.heading: The structure
bullets: Two strands twisted into a double helix
Bases pair: A with T, C with G
The order of bases is the code
teach.note: Show a 3D model. Ask: 'If one strand reads ATCG, what does the other read?' (TAGC).

teach.heading: The discovery
teach.note: Answer the big question as a discussion.

timeline.text: Chargaff: amounts of A = T and C = G
Franklin and Gosling take Photo 51 using X-rays
Watson and Crick build the double-helix model, using Franklin's data
Nobel Prize to Watson, Crick and Wilkins (Franklin died in 1958)

teach.heading: How science works
teach.note: The Nobel Prize is not given after death, but Franklin's role was underplayed for years.

misconception.right: DNA was known since 1869; they modelled its structure using others' data

check.q: One DNA strand reads A A G C T. What is the matching strand?
check.why: A pairs with T and G pairs with C: AAGCT → TTCGA.

practice: Name the four bases
What is the shape of DNA called?
What did Franklin's Photo 51 show?
independent: Core: Write a short biography of Rosalind Franklin's contribution
Extend: Explain how Watson and Crick used other scientists' data to build their model
Stretch: 'Credit in science should be shared by everyone who contributed.' Discuss, using the DNA story.
exit: What is the shape of DNA?
Name two scientists in the DNA story.
lessons.homework: Make a paper or sweet model of DNA showing base pairs correctly (photo to upload).
lessons.send: Support: base-pair cards. Stretch: how DNA codes for proteins.

lessons.unit: 9A: Genetics and evolution
lessons.title: Natural selection
lessons.bigQuestion: Why are antibiotics becoming less effective?
objectives: Describe the process of natural selection
Apply natural selection to examples such as peppered moths and bacteria
Describe Darwin's and Wallace's contributions
successCriteria: List the steps of natural selection
Explain antibiotic resistance using natural selection
Evaluate the evidence from peppered moths
lessons.crossCurricular: History: Darwin's voyage on HMS Beagle; Medicine: antibiotic resistance; Islamic Studies: Muslim scholars' views on science and creation
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: questions of science and faith; Muslim views on the origin of humans differ and are discussed in Islamic Studies, while natural selection in bacteria and moths is observed science

keywords.def: organisms better suited to their environment survive and reproduce more
a feature that helps an organism survive
a random change in DNA
bacteria no longer killed by an antibiotic

starter: Give an adaptation of a camel

teach.heading: The steps
teach.note: Use the cycle and repeat with each example.
cycle: Genes passed on; more common over time

teach.heading: Peppered moths
bullets: Pale moths camouflaged on clean bark
Soot darkened trees in industrial England
Dark moths survived better; then fell again after clean-air laws

teach.heading: Antibiotic resistance
bullets: A random mutation makes a bacterium resistant

model.problem: Explain how MRSA became resistant to antibiotics
steps: A mutation made one bacterium resistant
Antibiotics killed non-resistant bacteria
The resistant bacterium survived and reproduced
Resistant bacteria became common
model.answer: Natural selection of a resistant variant

misconception.wrong: Bacteria become resistant because they try to
misconception.right: Random mutations happen; resistant ones survive and reproduce

check.q: Why should patients finish their course of antibiotics?
options: So that all bacteria are killed and fewer resistant ones survive
Because the medicine tastes better later
check.why: Stopping early leaves the toughest bacteria alive to multiply. Finishing the course kills more.

practice: List the four steps of natural selection
Why did dark peppered moths increase?
What is a mutation?
independent: Core: Explain the peppered moth story in four steps
Extend: Explain how antibiotic resistance develops and two ways doctors slow it
Stretch: Darwin and Wallace both proposed natural selection in 1858. Explain why scientists working independently and reaching the same idea strengthens it.
exit: One way to reduce antibiotic resistance?
lessons.homework: Research one example of natural selection observed today (e.g. pesticide-resistant insects) and explain it in four steps.
lessons.send: Support: step cards to order. Stretch: Darwin and Wallace comparison.

lessons.unit: 9A: Genetics and evolution
lessons.title: Extinction and endangered species
lessons.bigQuestion: Does it matter if a species disappears forever?
objectives: Describe causes of extinction
Explain how genetic diversity helps species survive
Evaluate the effects of human activity on species
successCriteria: Name four causes of extinction
Explain why small populations are at greater risk
Evaluate whether humans have a duty to protect species
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: habitats and deforestation; Islamic Studies: animals as communities (Surah Al-An'am 6:38)
lessons.smsc: Moral and spiritual: animals are 'communities like you' (Al-An'am 6:38); stewardship (khalifah)

keywords.def: no members of the species are left alive
at risk of becoming extinct
the place where an organism lives
the variety of genes in a population

teach.heading: Causes of extinction
teach.note: Examples: dodo (hunting and introduced animals), passenger pigeon (over-hunting).

teach.heading: Small populations, big risk
bullets: A new disease may kill them all
Less variation for natural selection to work on

model.problem: Explain why cheetahs are at high risk from disease
steps: Cheetahs have very low genetic diversity
If a disease strikes, few may have resistance
Many could die, and the population could collapse
model.answer: Low diversity → less chance some survive a change

teach.heading: Does it matter?
teach.note: Answer the big question as a structured discussion.

teach.heading: Extinction vs endangered
teach.note: Example: the giant panda has improved from endangered to vulnerable.

misconception.right: Endangered means at risk; protection can help recovery

check.q: Why does low genetic diversity increase extinction risk?
options: Fewer individuals may have genes to survive a change
check.why: With less variation, a new disease or climate change may affect them all in the same way.

practice: Name three causes of extinction
What is genetic diversity?
Name an endangered species
independent: Core: Make a fact file on one endangered species: threats and protection
Extend: Explain why rainforest destruction leads to extinctions
Stretch: Write a balanced argument: should a country spend millions saving one species?
lessons.homework: Research one UK species that is endangered (e.g. the hedgehog or red squirrel) and one thing families can do to help.
lessons.send: Support: fact-file template. Stretch: population graphs.

lessons.unit: 9A: Genetics and evolution
lessons.title: Gene banks and conservation
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do scientists store millions of seeds in an Arctic vault?
objectives: Describe how gene banks preserve genetic material
Compare methods of conservation
Evaluate the use of gene banks
successCriteria: Describe seed banks and frozen tissue banks
Compare in-situ and ex-situ conservation
Evaluate strengths and limits of gene banks
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: food security; Food technology: crop varieties
lessons.smsc: Moral: planning for future generations

keywords.def: a store of genetic material such as seeds, sperm or tissue
a store of seeds kept cold and dry
protecting species and habitats
breeding endangered animals in zoos

starter: Why do seeds last a long time?

teach.heading: Gene banks
bullets: Svalbard Global Seed Vault in Norway holds over a million samples
teach.note: Answer the big question: a backup if crops are lost to war, disease or disaster. Seeds from the Middle East were withdrawn from Svalbard in 2015 after the Syrian war damaged a gene bank near Aleppo.

teach.heading: Conservation methods
bullets: In the wild (in situ) or away from it (ex situ)

right.title: Ex situ (away)
points: Backup if wild habitat is lost

model.problem: Evaluate seed banks as a way to save plant species
steps: Strength: store huge diversity safely for decades
Strength: can replant after a disaster
Limit: does not protect habitats or animals
Limit: stored seeds don't evolve with a changing climate
model.answer: Valuable backup, but must be combined with protecting habitats

teach.heading: Zoos alone are not enough
bullets: Captive animals may lose wild skills
teach.note: Release programmes need habitats to return to.

misconception.wrong: Keeping a species in zoos fully saves it
misconception.right: Without wild habitats and enough diversity, it remains at risk

check.q: Which is an example of ex-situ conservation?
check.why: A seed bank stores genetic material away from the natural habitat. The others protect species in the wild.

practice: What is a gene bank?
Give one in-situ method
Why keep seeds cold and dry?
independent: Core: Compare three conservation methods in a table
Extend: Explain why the Svalbard vault is in the Arctic
Stretch: Evaluate captive breeding of a named species (e.g. the Arabian oryx), including its reintroduction to the wild.
lessons.homework: Research the Arabian oryx and write a paragraph on how it was saved from extinction in the wild.
lessons.send: Support: comparison table frame. Stretch: oryx case study.

lessons.title: 9A review: genetics and evolution

objectives: Retrieve key knowledge from 9A
Apply it to new examples
Prepare for International GCSE Biology Section 3 (reproduction and inheritance)
successCriteria: Recall variation, genes and natural selection facts
Answer data questions

keywords.def: differences between organisms
section of DNA coding for a characteristic
better adapted organisms survive and reproduce
permanent loss of a species

bullets: Variation → genes → inheritance → selection → survival or extinction

model.problem: Explain how rats became resistant to the poison warfarin (6 marks)
steps: Variation: some rats had a mutation giving resistance
Warfarin killed non-resistant rats
Resistant rats survived and had less competition
They reproduced and passed on the resistance gene
Over generations, most rats became resistant
model.answer: Five linked steps applied to rats

misconception.wrong: Giraffes stretched their necks and passed on long necks
misconception.right: Giraffes with longer necks survived better and passed on genes for longer necks

check.q: Two plants grown from cuttings of one parent grow to different heights. The cause is…

practice: Explain environmental variation with an example
Describe DNA's structure
List steps of natural selection

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Making materials (9E); conservation of energy
lessons.title: About ceramics: properties and uses
lessons.bigQuestion: Why is a ceramic mug hard but easy to smash?
objectives: To understand how the properties of ceramics make them suited to their uses
successCriteria: All: name four properties of ceramics
Most: link each property to a use
Some: explain the difference between hard and tough
lessons.crossCurricular: Art and design: ceramic tiles and Islamic geometric tilework
lessons.smsc: Cultural: the tile traditions of Muslim civilisation (Iznik, Isfahan)

keywords.def: a hard material made by heating clay or other minerals
breaks suddenly without bending
resistance to scratching
does not conduct heat or electricity well
temperature at which a solid melts

hook.text: The tiles on a 500-year-old masjid in Isfahan still shine. What properties must those tiles have?
hook.a: Hard, unreactive, heat and water resistant, keep their colour: ceramics.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'He created the human being from clay like pottery' (ar-Rahman 55:14). Pottery, the oldest ceramic, is made by firing clay, and the Qur'an uses it to remind us of our own creation.

starter.q: Name the products of complete combustion of methane.

starter.a: A characteristic of a material, such as hardness.
For example: wood, plastic, air, wool.
Two or more elements chemically joined.

teach.heading: Property words
teach.note: Quick-fire: give a material for each property.

teach.heading: Ceramics
bullets: Made by heating clay to high temperature
teach.note: Answer the big question: ceramic mugs keep drinks hot and don't burn your hands.

teach.heading: Hard is not the same as tough

misconception.right: Ceramics are hard but brittle: they shatter when dropped

teach.heading: Justifying a choice
bullets: Property → why it helps the use

model.problem: Explain why ceramic is used for spark plug insulators in engines
steps: High melting point: survives engine heat
Electrical insulator: keeps the spark in the right place
Hard: resists wear
model.answer: Three properties linked to the job

check.q: Why are ceramic tiles used around cookers?
options: They have a high melting point and are easy to clean
check.why: Ceramics resist heat and glazed tiles are waterproof and easy to clean.

practice.q: Explain why porcelain is used for insulators on power lines.
practice.a: It is an electrical insulator, so current cannot flow through it to the pylon; it is also weather resistant.
practice.model:
Property: electrical insulator.
Use: holds live cables on metal pylons.
Link: current cannot pass through the porcelain into the pylon.
So porcelain keeps the pylon safe.

practice.q: Hard or tough: a ceramic plate?
practice.a: Hard but not tough (brittle).

practice.q: Why are ceramics used to line ovens and kilns?
practice.a: High melting point and thermal insulators.

independent.q: Core: Make a table of five ceramic objects at home (mug, plate, tile, sink, brick): property used and why.
independent.a: For example: mug: hard, waterproof, insulator; tile: hard, easy to clean, heat resistant.
independent.model: Teacher fills the first row: mug: hard, waterproof when glazed, poor conductor so the handle stays cool.

independent.q: Extend: Explain why ceramics shatter but metals bend (portal response box).
independent.a: Ceramic particles are held rigidly and cannot slide, so cracks spread; metal layers can slide, so metals bend.

independent.q: Stretch: Why are ceramic tiles used on the underside of some spacecraft?
independent.a: They withstand extreme temperatures on re-entry and are excellent thermal insulators.

exit.q: Ceramics are...
exit.a: Hard but brittle

exit.q: Big question: why is a ceramic mug hard but easy to smash?
exit.a: Ceramics resist scratching but their particles cannot slide, so they crack and shatter.

lessons.homework: Find a ceramic object at home and write three properties that make it suitable for its job.
lessons.send: SEND: property word bank with pictures. EAL: brittle, hard, tough. Stretch: compare glass and porcelain as ceramics.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Making materials (9E); conservation of energy
lessons.title: Testing hardness safely at home
lessons.bigQuestion: How can we rank materials by hardness without a laboratory?
objectives: To understand how a scratch test compares the hardness of materials
successCriteria: All: carry out a scratch test safely
Most: rank materials using a hardness scale
Some: evaluate the reliability of the scratch test
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: the Mohs scale used to identify rocks and minerals
lessons.smsc: Moral: honesty in recording results

keywords.def: a 1 to 10 scale ranking minerals by scratch hardness
a test to see which material scratches which
getting similar results when repeated
put in order
resistance to scratching

hook.text: Diamond scratches everything. What scratches diamond?
hook.a: Only another diamond: it is 10 on the Mohs scale.

teach.heading: The Mohs idea
bullets: A harder material scratches a softer one

teach.heading: Our test
bullets: Try fingernail, then coin, then steel key
Record the softest tester that scratches
teach.note: Use soap, chalk, a candle, a ceramic tile (unglazed back), a plastic lid.

teach.heading: Safety
bullets: Press gently, away from your hand
Wipe marks: is it a scratch or a smear?

teach.heading: Common error
bullets: A mark is not always a scratch

misconception.wrong: Any mark means the material was scratched
misconception.right: Rub the mark: a streak wipes off; a scratch is a groove you can feel

check.q: A coin scratches a material but a fingernail does not. Its Mohs hardness is between...
check.why: Harder than a fingernail (2.5) but softer than the coin (3.5).

practice.q: The steel key scratches a tile but the coin does not. Estimate the tile's hardness.
practice.a: Between 3.5 and 5.5.
practice.model:
The coin (3.5) cannot scratch it, so it is harder than 3.5.
The key (5.5) can, so it is softer than 5.5.
So between 3.5 and 5.5.

practice.q: Why test with the softest tester first?
practice.a: So we find the lowest tester that scratches, without damaging the sample more than needed.

practice.q: What does a streak that wipes off show?
practice.a: The tester left material behind; it is not a scratch.

independent.q: Core: Scratch-test five household materials with a fingernail, a coin and a steel key. Record and rank them.
independent.a: Pupils' own, e.g. soap and candle softest, plastic, then tile hardest.
independent.model: Teacher tests soap on camera: fingernail scratches it, so it is below 2.5.

independent.q: Extend: Explain why the unglazed back of a tile is harder to scratch than plastic.
independent.a: Ceramic particles are held by strong bonds in a rigid structure; plastic chains can be pushed apart.

independent.q: Stretch: Evaluate your test: how could you make it more reliable?
independent.a: Same pressure each time, repeat each test, use a magnifying glass to check grooves, more testers between values.

exit.q: Diamond is ... on the Mohs scale.
Big question: how can we rank materials by hardness without a laboratory?
exit.a: A scratch test with testers of known hardness, then order the results.

lessons.homework: Write up your scratch test: method, results table, ranking and one improvement.
lessons.send: SEND: three materials only, results grid. EAL: scratch, groove, rank. Stretch: research why diamond is so hard.

lessons.title: From clay to ceramic: firing and structure
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does soft, wet clay become hard pottery in a kiln?
objectives: To understand how heating changes the structure of clay to make a ceramic
successCriteria: All: describe the steps from clay to fired pottery
Most: explain that firing removes water and joins particles
Some: explain why firing is a chemical, not a physical, change
lessons.crossCurricular: History: pottery of early civilisations and the potters of Muslim Spain
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: reflecting on creation from clay

keywords.def: fine-grained earth that is soft when wet
a very hot oven for firing pottery
heating clay to make it hard
a glassy coating that makes pottery waterproof
cannot be changed back

hook.text: Dried clay can be softened again with water. Fired clay cannot. What has changed?
hook.a: Firing at high temperature causes chemical changes that bond the particles permanently.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'He created the human being from clay like pottery' (ar-Rahman 55:14). Pottery, the oldest ceramic, is made by firing clay, and the Qur'an uses it to remind us of our own creation.

starter.q: A coin scratches it, a fingernail does not. Hardness?
Name a ceramic in your kitchen.

teach.heading: Making pottery
bullets: Fire in a kiln at about 1000 °C
teach.note: Teacher shows a photograph of a kiln.

teach.heading: What firing does
bullets: Removes water bonded in the clay
teach.note: Fired clay is a new material: a chemical change.

teach.heading: Reversible or not?
bullets: Dried clay: water added back softens it
Fired clay: water cannot undo it

teach.heading: Glaze
teach.note: Unglazed flower pots let water through; glazed mugs do not.

check.q: Why is firing a chemical change?
options: New bonds form and it cannot be reversed
check.why: Firing makes a new material that cannot be turned back into clay.

practice.q: Put in order: glaze, shape, fire, dry.
practice.a: Shape, dry, fire, glaze (then fire again).
practice.model:
First you need a shape: shape.
It must lose water slowly: dry.
Then make it hard: fire.
Finally seal it: glaze, then fire again.

practice.q: Why do unglazed flower pots feel damp?
practice.a: They are porous, so water soaks through.

practice.q: Why dry clay slowly before firing?
practice.a: So water does not turn to steam inside and crack it.

independent.q: Core: Put a spoonful of soil or flour paste on two saucers: leave one to dry, add water to the other after drying. Record what happens and link it to clay.

keywords.def: energy in the store of a stretched or squashed object
how much longer something is when stretched
the point after which it will not return to its shape
a device that pushes an object off
a line showing the trend in data

hook.text: A bow stores energy when pulled back. Where does that energy come from, and where does it go?
hook.a: From the archer's muscles (chemical store) into the bow's elastic store, then into the arrow's kinetic store.

starter.q: KE of a 2 kg object at 4 m/s?
Energy is conserved. What does that mean?

teach.heading: Elastic store
teach.note: Archery was encouraged by the Prophet (peace be upon him); a bow is an elastic store.

teach.heading: The launcher
bullets: Elastic band between two chair legs
Pull a toy car back by set distances
teach.note: Safety: aim along the floor, away from people and animals; wear glasses if available.

check.q: When the band is released, energy is transferred from...
check.why: The stretched band's elastic store transfers energy to the car's kinetic store.

practice.q: Describe the energy transfers from pulling the band to the car stopping.
practice.a: Chemical (muscles) to elastic (band) to kinetic (car) to thermal (friction) and sound.
practice.model:
Start: muscles (chemical store) do work stretching the band.
Band: elastic store.
Release: car's kinetic store.
Stopping: friction dissipates it to thermal stores of car, floor and air.

practice.q: From the graph, is distance proportional to pull-back?
practice.a: No: it increases faster than in proportion (curve).

practice.q: Why repeat each pull-back three times?
practice.a: To spot anomalies and calculate a mean.

independent.q: Core: Carry out the launcher test at 4 pull-back distances, three repeats each. Record and calculate means.
independent.a: Pupils' own; distance increases with pull-back.
independent.model: Teacher shows the first test on camera: pull back 2 cm against a ruler, release, measure the roll with a tape measure.

independent.q: Extend: Plot your means and draw a line of best fit. Describe the pattern.
independent.a: Distance increases as pull-back increases, more steeply at larger pull-backs.

independent.q: Stretch: Why might very large pull-backs give smaller distances than expected?
independent.a: The band may pass its elastic limit, or the car may skid or spin, wasting energy.

exit.q: A stretched band stores energy in its... store.
exit.a: Elastic

exit.q: Big question: does stretching an elastic band further make a toy car go further?
exit.a: Yes: more extension stores more elastic energy, transferred to more kinetic energy.

lessons.homework: Write up the launcher investigation with a graph and conclusion.

hook.a: Energy used depends on power and time; the heater's power is hundreds of times higher.

teach.heading: Comparing costs

practice.q: Cost of 12 kWh at 25p per kWh?

independent.model: Teacher does the kettle first: 3 kW, about 12 minutes a day = 0.2 h; 0.6 kWh; 0.6 × 25 = 15p.

exit.a: 4 kWh

exit.a: About 5p for a 4-minute boil of a 3 kW kettle at 25p per kWh.

hook.a: Energy becomes spread out (dissipated) as thermal energy, which we cannot easily use again.
